title: Symphony No. 2 in E minor
hook: The symphony Rachmaninoff dared to write ten years after his first one failed.

painting.title: The Emerald Necklace
painting.pairingNote: Young women in old-fashioned dresses in a deep green summer garden, a dream of the Russian past painted a few years before the symphony; the same long, wistful lyricism.

facts: In 1897 the premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony was a disaster, and for three years he could hardly compose. The Second Piano Concerto (1901) restored his confidence, but a new symphony was the real test.

In 1906 he moved with his family to Dresden, away from the busy musical life and the political unrest of Moscow, to have time to compose. He wrote the Second Symphony there between October 1906 and April 1907 and dedicated it to his old teacher Sergei Taneyev.
He conducted the first performance himself in St Petersburg in February 1908. It was a success, and later that year it won him a Glinka Award.

For decades the symphony was usually played with large cuts, sometimes down to about 35 minutes. Since around 1970 the complete text has become the norm. This recording plays it complete, without the first-movement repeat.
A short, dark [[motto|motto]] from the opening returns in every movement and ties the four together.
bigPicture.inOneLine: shadows that slowly lift (I), a galloping [[scherzo|scherzo]] (II), a long love song (III), a festival (IV).

movements.heading: Largo – Allegro moderato
movements.summary: A slow, dark introduction grows from a few notes in the cellos and basses. When the faster main section begins, its first theme turns out to be made from the same notes. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with a stormy development and a coda that ends in E minor with two loud outbursts.

mainIdeas.name: The motto
mainIdeas.description: a short, sighing phrase rising and falling in the low strings, heard at the very start.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a restless, surging violin melody, built from the motto.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a gentle, swaying melody in the major, over soft [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] in the lower strings.

stops.hear: Cellos and basses alone, very low and quiet; soft chords in the winds answer
stops.happening: The motto, in the slow introduction

stops.hear: The violins take up the phrase; the music thickens and swells to a climax, then sinks back
A solo English horn plays a melancholy line over hushed strings
stops.happening: The bridge to the faster main section

stops.hear: The tempo picks up; the violins play a restless, surging tune
stops.happening: The Allegro moderato: Theme 1, from the motto

stops.hear: Calmer: woodwinds and strings share a gentle, swaying melody; the low strings are plucked
Faster and stormier; fragments of the motto and Theme 1 are tossed around, a solo violin breaks through
A long build to a huge climax; Theme 1 returns at full strength
The swaying melody returns, now warmer, in E major
The pace quickens; brass and timpani drive the music on

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Two loud, abrupt outbursts in E minor
stops.happening: The movement ends in the minor, not in triumph

notice: Listen to the first ten seconds and remember the phrase in the low strings. It will come back in every movement.
Theme 2 is in the major the first time and again at its return. Compare its warmth with the dark key of the ending.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Simon Rattle, then the London Symphony Orchestra’s music director, conducted the symphony from memory at the opening concerts of the orchestra’s 2019–20 season at the Barbican.

movements.heading: Allegro molto
movements.summary: A fast, energetic movement in the role of a [[scherzo|scherzo]], though in two beats rather than three. A galloping horn tune alternates with a broad, singing melody; in the middle comes a busy section where the instruments chase one another. At the end the brass quietly play a chant-like phrase, and the music vanishes.

mainIdeas.name: The galloping tune
mainIdeas.description: a bold horn melody over a rushing [[ostinato|ostinato]] in the strings. It is related to the medieval chant [[dies-irae|Dies irae]].

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a broad, warm melody for the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The chase
mainIdeas.description: quick, overlapping entries in the middle section, like a [[fugato|fugato]].

stops.hear: The strings rush in a fast, repeating pattern; the horns call out a bold tune
stops.happening: The main section, with the horn tune

stops.hear: Everything relaxes; the violins sing a broad, warm melody
stops.happening: The lyrical second idea, in C major

stops.hear: The rushing strings and the horn tune return
A sudden, loud chord; then quick figures chase each other through the orchestra
The chase grows louder and harder-edged, then winds down
stops.happening: The middle section reaches its peak

stops.hear: The galloping horn tune and rushing strings return
The violins’ warm melody comes back

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The brass play a slow, quiet, chant-like phrase; the music fades to almost nothing
stops.happening: A soft ending. The chant-like phrase returns at the end of the finale

notice: Count the beats in the galloping tune: two in a bar, not the three of most scherzos.
Remember the quiet brass phrase at the end. It comes back, loud, in the last minute of the symphony.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: One of the best-loved slow movements in the repertoire. After a short, yearning phrase in the violins, a solo clarinet sings a long, winding melody that seems never to end. The motto returns in the middle and leads to a climax; then the melodies return, interwoven.

mainIdeas.name: The violins’ phrase
mainIdeas.description: a short, rising, yearning line that opens the movement.

mainIdeas.name: The clarinet song
mainIdeas.description: a long melody that circles around single notes and keeps unfolding.
The motto from the first movement, now gentler.

stops.hear: The violins play a short, rising, yearning phrase over warm chords
stops.happening: The opening theme, in A major

stops.hear: A solo clarinet begins a long, slow, winding melody
stops.happening: The clarinet solo, the heart of the movement

stops.hear: The strings and then the oboe and English horn take the music further
stops.happening: The melody passes through the orchestra

stops.hear: The motto appears in the woodwinds and strings; the music becomes restless and searching
stops.happening: The middle section, built on the motto

stops.hear: A long swell to a loud, glowing climax
The violins sing the clarinet’s melody; the opening phrase weaves around it
A last echo of the motto, softly

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Quiet strings; the music fades on a calm A major chord

notice: Follow the clarinet solo from start to finish. It lasts around two minutes without a real pause.
When the clarinet’s melody returns in the violins, listen for the opening phrase woven around it in other instruments.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The clarinet solo is played by the orchestra’s principal clarinettist, Chris Richards.

movements.heading: Allegro vivace
movements.summary: A bright, festive finale in E major. A galloping first theme, a march, and then one of Rachmaninoff’s broadest melodies. Themes from the earlier movements reappear, and the symphony ends in a blaze of E major.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a quick, leaping, festive tune in the full orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a short, tripping episode in the woodwinds.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a broad, sweeping melody in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The falling scale
mainIdeas.description: long descending scales, like peals of bells, in the development.

stops.hear: The full orchestra bursts in with a quick, leaping, festive tune
A light, tripping march in the woodwinds
The festive tune returns
The strings sing a broad, sweeping melody
Over shimmering string [[tremolo|tremolo]], a quiet memory of the slow movement’s opening phrase
Abrupt flashes of the scherzo’s and the first movement’s themes
New, restless ideas, passed around the orchestra
Long scales descending again and again, piling up like bells
stops.happening: The development, second part, built on a falling scale

stops.hear: The festive Theme 1 returns
The broad string melody returns in E major, now at full strength, with the whole orchestra
A fast, whirling dash; the brass blaze out the chant-like phrase from the scherzo

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Loud chords in a short, strong rhythm
stops.happening: The symphony ends in E major

notice: Theme 2 appears twice: in D major in the middle and in E major near the end. Notice how much grander it is the second time.
The brass chant at the very end is the same phrase that ended the scherzo quietly. Here it is loud and triumphant.

threads.title: The motto
threads.body: The low-string phrase of the opening returns in all four movements, darker or gentler, and links them into one story.

threads.title: From E minor to E major
threads.body: The first movement ends in the minor. The finale turns the same key to the major and ends in celebration.

threads.title: Long melodies
threads.body: The clarinet’s song in the Adagio and the broad string tune of the finale keep unfolding, the hallmark of Rachmaninoff’s style.

threads.title: A comeback
threads.body: After the failure of the First Symphony, this symphony’s success confirmed Rachmaninoff as a composer of large orchestral works.
